name: Iris Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy fresh fruit, veg and chilled goods for Greenmile Foodservice, which supplies restaurants, school kitchens and care homes. I'm up at five, check overnight market prices, and place the day's orders by seven. Then it's a lot of chasing growers about quality, and juggling what's cheap against what the chefs will actually accept. I love it, honestly, it's like a fast game with real tomatoes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Marco is an electrician, so he's up on ladders while I'm up on spreadsheets. We have Lucia, who's twelve, and Mateo, who's nine, and a mortgage we stretched for. I'm 43 and I'm still one of the juniors on the buying team, since I only moved over from dispatch three years ago and I'm still learning the growers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, not magic. At work I'd tell the team it saves me an hour a day on price comparisons, and that's about it. Online I'd probably post a tip about how I use it for the supplier spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a plateau would suit me. I'd stay the person on the buying team who gets the most out of the tools, and that helps a junior like me. Greenmile is doing well, the chefs want fresh local produce, and I feel pretty settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, a bit more AI each month. I'd try an AI tool for predicting how much lettuce the care homes need, because we waste about eight percent of leafy veg. I'd put money into the kids' savings and keep paying the mortgage as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels comfortable, which I'm slightly suspicious of. I'd be calm, but I'd keep a small voice saying don't get lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI every day. What do you actually ask it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I put the weekly price sheet in and ask it which growers have gone up unusually, or I ask it to write a polite but firm email about a bad delivery of peppers. It also translates when a grower from abroad writes in broken English. I always check numbers myself, because it once told me a price was in kilos when it was in crates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what would stay a worry even if AI went nowhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, honestly. We stretched for the house when my daughter Lucia was small and rates have squeezed us since. And fresh produce margins are thin, so if one big customer leaves I'd feel it. But that's normal life, not AI.

say: I'd say it's a **useful tool**, not magic, and saves me an hour a day.
I'd post a tip on how I use it for supplier spreadsheets.
think: A plateau suits me, because my **tool skills** set me apart on the buying team.
Greenmile is doing well and I feel fairly settled.
do: Try an AI tool to forecast lettuce demand for the **care homes**.
Keep adding a bit more AI to my routine each month.
Put money into the kids' savings and pay the mortgage as usual.
feel: Comfortable, with a small voice saying **don't get lazy**.
S0.quote: We stretched for the house when my daughter Lucia was small and rates have squeezed us since.
fieldNote: Genuinely sees a plateau as good for her; her **skills** are a small edge.
Names ordinary pressures, the mortgage and thin produce margins, but not as dread.

steps.text: Try an AI tool to forecast lettuce orders for care homes
Ask AI to flag growers whose prices jumped this week
Put a little more into the kids' savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change the job a lot and the people who learn it early will do fine. At work I'd offer to run a lunch session on how I use it. Online I'd say it's the first time I've seen a tool change my work this fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the repeat orders and the price tracking go to software within three or four years. That's maybe half of my day. What's left is relationships with growers and judging quality, which still needs a human, but there'll be fewer of us doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person who builds the automatic ordering for Greenmile, so I'm not being replaced by it. I'd do an online course in data analysis in the evenings, and I'd start helping two small cafes with their ordering on weekends for a bit of side money. In the first year I'd get a title change to buyer proper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and a bit scary, like when I moved from dispatch. I know I'd have to run faster than the colleague next to me, which tires me out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks do you think the software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Repeat orders and price tracking, no doubt. The software can already see weather, demand and growers' prices at once, which I can't. I'd say my only edge is knowing that a particular grower's strawberries are always better on Thursdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move on from Greenmile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they cut the team without telling us what's next, I'd move. A bigger distributor, or one of the grocery start-ups that sell direct to restaurants. I'd rather jump than be pushed, and my partner Marco says as an electrician he'd always find work, so we could risk a gap.

say: I'd offer a **lunch session** on how I use the tools.
I'd say this is the first tool I've seen change work this fast.
think: Repeat orders and price tracking, about **half my day**, will go to software within three or four years.
Grower relationships and judging quality still need a person, but with fewer people.
do: Become the person who builds Greenmile's **automatic ordering**.
Take an evening data analysis course.
Help two small cafes with ordering on weekends for extra money.
feel: Exciting and a bit scary, like **moving** from dispatch.
S1.quote: I'd rather jump than be pushed, and my partner Marco says as an electrician he'd always find work, so we could risk a gap.
fieldNote: Adaptive: wants to **build** the automation rather than be replaced by it.
Marco's electrician work gives her the confidence to risk a gap between jobs.

steps.text: Offer to build Greenmile's automatic reorder system
Take an evening data analysis course
Help two small cafes with weekend ordering for pay
Look at direct-to-restaurant food start-ups if the team is cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to learn how to work with it right now, and the firm should pay for it. At work I'd call a team meeting and ask what the plan is. Online I'd say we should not pretend it's slow, because it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think this is the one where my buying job disappears. Thinking work gets done by a machine better and cheaper, and I'm a junior with three years in the role. I'd be one of the first to go, even though I'm good with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use these two years like a sprint. I'd move my side work with the cafes up to a proper small business advising kitchens on ordering with AI, and I'd save every spare pound. I'd also ask Greenmile to move me to handling grower relationships and quality checks, which are hands-on and slower to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a rush of adrenaline with a lump of fear underneath. I'm not frozen, I'm moving, but I wake at four wondering about school fees and the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What do you say to your boss that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my boss, tell me honestly which roles you're keeping, and I'll tell you which I want. I'd ask for a proper retraining budget, and I'd ask them to share the savings the AI makes. I'd want a person to say it to my face, not a mass email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hold on to about the hands-on side of food buying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walking the market in person still matters, and robots take another three years or so to do that. So I'd shift to the field work, visiting growers, checking boxes and cold chains. It's less glamorous but it buys time, and Marco keeps earning meanwhile.

say: I'd say we should **not pretend** it's slow, because it isn't.
I'd call a team meeting and ask what the plan is.
think: This is the one where my buying job **disappears**, and as a junior I'd be early.
I'm good with the tools, but a machine does thinking work cheaper.
do: Turn my cafe side work into a small business advising kitchens on **AI ordering**.
Ask Greenmile to move me to grower visits and quality checks.
feel: An **adrenaline** rush with a lump of fear; I wake at four.
S2.quote: I'd say to my boss, tell me honestly which roles you're keeping, and I'll tell you which I want.
fieldNote: Stays active under pressure, but the **fear** shows up at four in the morning.
Sees the three-year robot gap as a reason to move into field visits and quality checks.

steps.text: Turn the cafe side work into a paid ordering advice business
Save every spare pound towards the mortgage and school costs
Ask Greenmile to move me to grower visits and quality checks
Use AI to prepare orders for the cafe clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enough time to learn it properly, so everyone should start now. At work I'd say let's build the new system ourselves. With friends I'd say the ones who keep trying will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel anxious but hopeful. Five years is enough for me to build a small advisory business and train for something else, and Marco's work isn't going anywhere for eight. If I do the right things, I could even be better off than now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year learning the data side, probably a certificate in supply chain analytics, and getting more AI work done at Greenmile. By year two I'd have three or four cafes paying me for advice. I'd also move the mortgage to a lower rate when I can and build six months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a challenge, which is better than dread. I'd still have bad nights, but mostly I'd feel busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years: what does that buy you compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can plan a pivot rather than panic. In two years I'd have no choice, here I could pick a path. I'd even consider starting a small firm that does ordering for food places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are Lucia and Mateo going to hear from you about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the world is changing and mum is learning along with it. I'd show Lucia how I use AI, because she's twelve and already knows more than I do. I'd say school matters, but so does being curious and not scared.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if everyone starts now.
I'd suggest we build the new ordering system ourselves.
think: Five years lets me build an **advisory side business** while Marco's work stays steady.
I could even be better off than now if I do the right things.
do: Study a supply chain **analytics** certificate in year one.
Grow to three or four paying cafe clients by year two.
Build six months of savings and refinance the mortgage.
feel: Like a **challenge**, which beats dread, with the odd bad night.
S3.quote: Five years means I can plan a pivot rather than panic. In two years I'd have no choice, here I could pick a path.
fieldNote: Time converts directly into a **plan**: analytics course, side clients and a firm of her own.
Plans to bring her daughter Lucia into her learning, a nice sign of her optimism.

steps.text: Study a supply chain analytics certificate in year one
Sign three or four cafes as paying advice clients
Refinance the mortgage and build six months of savings
Show Lucia how I use AI tools at home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, so use it. At work I'd carry on, but keep pushing for AI training for every buyer. Online I'd say it's the best time to start learning anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel quite calm about my own job. By 2036 I'd be 53 and I could have built something solid, while the kids finish school before the robots reach hands-on work in 2039. The thing I'd keep thinking about is whether everyone else gets the same chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on learning and slowly shift toward advising and running a small ordering service. I'd also invest in the kids' education and pay the mortgage down quickly. I'd probably keep my Greenmile job for years while the side business grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels light, almost like being given an extra decade. I'd still check the news every day, but I'd sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What risk would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The risk is that not everyone moves. My colleagues who don't use the tools and aren't curious worry me, because ten years is long but not infinite. I'd try to bring a few of them along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could change one thing now to prepare, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the data course this year instead of next. It's the thing that turns a good buyer into someone who can run the system. I'd also have the kids do a bit of coding and tinkering, so they aren't afraid of it.

say: I'd say a decade is **a gift**, so use it.
I'd keep pushing for AI training for every buyer.
think: I'd feel **calm** about my own job and worry about colleagues who don't move.
By 2036 I'd be 53 with the kids finished at school.
do: Shift slowly toward running a small **ordering service** while keeping my job.
Start the data course this year, not next.
feel: **Light**, like being given an extra decade.
S4.quote: The risk is that not everyone moves. My colleagues who don't use the tools and aren't curious worry me, because ten years is long but not infinite.
fieldNote: Her worry is for **colleagues** who won't change, not for herself or her own job.
Mentions the kids' early tinkering with code as part of the family plan, which shows her optimism.

steps.text: Start the data analysis course this year
Grow the ordering side service while keeping the Greenmile job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything, and Marco's income would be carrying us for a stretch. What would help is time-limited support while you retrain, and firms that tell staff early which jobs they're keeping.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I enjoy. I love the market and the people, the grower who texts me a photo of his tomatoes. I don't want to lose the market and the growers, even if I'm the one who built the machine that does half my job.

headlineQuote: I don't want to lose the market and the growers, even if I'm the one who built the machine that does half my job.
portrait: Iris, 43, is a **junior buyer** of fresh food for Greenmile Foodservice, with an electrician partner, two children and a mortgage.
She uses AI every day and tries to be the person who builds the new system, not the one it replaces.
She turns time into plans: data courses, side clients, savings and a shift toward hands-on grower work.
Her mood swings from calm in mild worlds to alarmed when AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because there's no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: **Time-limited support** while retraining, and firms that say early which jobs they're keeping.
